title: What to observe in LLM systems
summary: LLM systems fail quietly: the request succeeds, the text is fluent and the content is wrong. Observability records the shape of every run (spans, tokens, finish reasons, tool calls) and treats content as a separate, governed decision.
useIf: You operate, or are about to operate, a model-backed feature and need to explain wrong answers, slow runs and surprising bills.
avoidIf: You expect status codes and error rates alone to tell you whether the system works.

explain.md: A classic service fails loudly with a 500, a timeout or an exception. An LLM system usually returns 200. Error rates stay flat while answer quality drops, cost scales with tokens, latency depends on how many model and tool calls a run made, and the evidence you need to debug (the prompt, the retrieved text, the tool result) is also the data you must protect. That is why observability here has more jobs than uptime.

explain.caption: What changes compared with a classic service
head: Question
Classic service
LLM or agent system
Signal that answers it
rows: Often no: 200 with a wrong answer
Several model and tool calls per run, plus waits
Per token, varies with context, cache and reasoning
Token usage counters by model and agent
Prompts, retrieved chunks, tool arguments and results
Opt-in content capture, held outside the span
Model, prompt or data changes shift quality silently
Sampled online evaluation, scheduled test sets

explain.md: The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions give a shared vocabulary for the shape: spans such as `chat`, `invoke_agent` and `execute_tool`, token and duration metrics, and opt-in content attributes. All of them carry the status **Development** as of 2026-10-13, so pin versions and expect renames [[r1]]. Agent Framework emits these spans and metrics for you once telemetry is on [[r10]], and Foundry can collect traces server-side into Application Insights [[r12]].

explain.title: Shape first, content second
explain.md: Spans, token counts, finish reasons and tool-call counts rarely contain personal data and answer most operational questions. Prompts and outputs answer the rest but need consent, redaction, retention limits and access control. Decide them separately (see content capture, redaction and privacy).

whereToUse: A support assistant whose answers are fluent but sometimes wrong and nobody can say why
An agent platform where one user request fans out into many model and tool calls
A cost review after a token bill rose without a matching traffic increase
A release gate that needs to know whether a prompt change moved quality or latency
An incident where a downstream tool or MCP server failed silently inside an agent run

use: Trace every agent run end to end with model, tool and agent spans before launch
Emit token and duration metrics, which are not sampled, for dashboards and alerts
Score a sample of live traffic for quality so silent failures become visible
avoid: Do not rely on HTTP error rates as the health signal for answer quality
Do not capture prompts and outputs everywhere by default
Do not build dashboards on metric names you have not checked against what your build emits
flips: Data is regulated: keep shape signals in the main pipeline and move content to a separate, access-controlled store
Traffic is tiny and non-critical: console or local traces may be enough until you launch
Quality matters more than uptime for the feature: invest in online scoring before extra infrastructure dashboards

pitfalls.symptom: The answer was wrong, yet every span is green and the error rate is flat
pitfalls.cause: Only transport status was monitored, and quality is a semantic property
pitfalls.fix: Add run-level attributes (finish reasons, tool-call counts) and sampled online quality scores

pitfalls.symptom: A cost panel disagrees with the provider bill
pitfalls.cause: Cached and reasoning tokens were added on top of input and output totals, or sampled spans were summed
pitfalls.fix: Treat cached and reasoning counts as subsets and build totals from unsampled counters [[r5]]

pitfalls.symptom: Debugging requires prompts that nobody is allowed to store
pitfalls.cause: Content capture was an all-or-nothing switch
pitfalls.fix: Store content in a governed external store and keep references on spans [[r4]]

scenarios.title: Fluent but wrong, and no way to say why
scenarios.situation: A support assistant sometimes quotes the wrong policy. Error rates and latency are normal. The team has only HTTP logs. Customer data is involved and legal has not approved storing prompts.
constraints: No approval to store content yet
unknowns: How many model and tool calls does a run make?
Is retrieval the suspect or the model?
Can a restricted store hold content later?
scenarios.question: What do you add first?

options.name: Run traces with agent, model, retrieval and tool spans plus finish reasons and token counts, content off
options.why: It shows which step ran, how long it took and whether retrieval returned anything, without storing text.
options.tradeoff: You cannot read the wrong answer itself until a governed content store is approved.

options.name: Log full prompts and answers to the application log
options.why: It stores customer data without approval and is hard to correlate across steps.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a lab with synthetic data.

options.name: Add a weekly offline evaluation run
options.why: It measures quality on a golden set and catches regressions.
options.tradeoff: It does not explain live failures or see unseen inputs.

flips.if: Legal approves a restricted store with short retention
flips.then: Add content capture by reference for sampled and failed runs.

flips.if: The data is synthetic or internal only
flips.then: Capture content on spans in non-production.

scenarios.takeaway: Start with run shape, which is safe and answers most questions.

scenarios.title: The bill doubled while traffic did not
scenarios.situation: Monthly token spend doubled. Request volume grew 10 percent. Three teams share one model deployment through a gateway.
constraints: Need attribution by team and agent
unknowns: Did context length or reasoning usage grow?
scenarios.question: Which signal do you build first?

options.name: Token usage counters by model and agent, plus inference-call counts per run
options.why: Counters are unsampled and show whether tokens per call or calls per run rose.
options.tradeoff: Needs careful dimension choices to avoid cardinality blowups.

options.name: Sampled trace review
options.why: Good for explaining a spike once you know where to look.

options.name: Request-count dashboard
options.why: Requests barely changed, so it cannot explain the spike.
options.tradeoff: Useful as a denominator for tokens per request.

flips.then: Emit token metrics at the gateway with a team dimension.

flips.if: One agent shows rising calls per run
flips.then: Inspect its traces for a loop or retry storm.

scenarios.takeaway: Use unsampled counters for totals and traces for explanations.

quiz.q: Why can an LLM feature be broken while its error rate and latency look healthy?
options: The request returns success even when the answer is wrong, so quality needs its own signals
Latency does not matter for LLM systems
Token counts hide the error rate
quiz.explain: Transport success says nothing about semantic correctness, so you need online quality scoring and run-level signals. LLM clients do raise errors, latency does matter and token counts are unrelated to error rates.

quiz.q: Which signals are generally safe to collect for every run without storing user content? Select all that apply.
options: Token usage counts and finish reasons
Full prompt and response text on every span
Agent, model and tool span names and durations
quiz.explain: Shape signals (counts, durations, names, finish reasons) rarely contain personal data. Full prompts and responses are the sensitive part and are opt-in under the GenAI conventions.

flashcards.front: Why is HTTP success not enough for an LLM feature?
flashcards.back: A 200 response can carry a fluent but wrong answer. You need run-level signals and sampled quality scoring as well.

flashcards.front: Which signals describe the shape of a run?
flashcards.back: Spans for agent, model and tool steps, token usage, durations, finish reasons and tool-call counts.
